entries.meaning: To set money or resources aside for one specific purpose. ---
examples: Congress may earmark funds for rural clinics.
The city earmarked two million dollars for repairs.
That land has been earmarked for housing.
entries.contrast: Earmark takes for: earmarked for research.

entries.meaning: To move little by little in one direction, or to form a border along something. ---
examples: Prices edge higher every month.
He edged toward the exit without a word.
She was edging along the narrow ledge.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (edge toward the door), transitive (edge the lawn)
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: edge → edging.

entries.meaning: To mix personal opinion into what is supposed to be a factual report. ---
examples: Reporters should not editorialize in a news story.
The anchor editorialized about the mayor for two minutes.
Critics said the paper was editorializing on its front page.
entries.contrast: American spelling ends in -ize; British writes editorialise.

entries.meaning: To bring something about, especially a change. ---
examples: Only Congress can effect a change this large.
The new director effected a complete turnaround.
Reforms have been effected at every level.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with affect. To affect something is to influence it; to effect something is to make it happen. Effect is usually the noun (эффект) and only rarely this verb.

entries.meaning: To supply something with electric power, or to excite a crowd suddenly. ---
examples: The state plans to electrify the whole rail line.
Her performance electrified the audience.
The village was electrified only in 1974.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: electrifies, electrified, but electrifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To kill or badly injure someone with an electric shock. ---
examples: A downed line can electrocute anyone who touches it.
The fault nearly electrocuted a technician.
Two workers were electrocuted at the site.

entries.meaning: To draw a response, answer, or reaction out of someone. ---
examples: Good questions elicit honest answers.
The ad elicited hundreds of complaints.
So far the letter has elicited no response.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with the adjective illicit (незаконный), which sounds almost identical.

entries.meaning: To make something longer, or to grow longer. ---
examples: Heels elongate the line of the leg.
The shadows elongated as the sun dropped.
The cells become elongated as they mature.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (elongate the shape), intransitive (the shadows elongate)

entries.meaning: To make something clear by explaining it carefully. ---
examples: The footnotes elucidate the author's sources.
She elucidated the theory with a simple diagram.
The paper has elucidated a mechanism no one understood.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (elucidate the point), intransitive (he declined to elucidate)

entries.meaning: To escape or avoid someone, or to stay beyond someone's reach or understanding. ---
examples: The right word can elude you for hours.
The suspect eluded police for a week.
The prize has eluded her three years running.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with allude (to mention indirectly): he alluded to the problem, but a solution eluded him.

entries.meaning: To come out from a source, or to give off a quality or feeling. ---
examples: Strange noises emanate from the basement at night.
A faint smell of smoke emanated from the kitchen.
The order turned out to have emanated from the mayor's office.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive (light emanates from it), transitive (she emanates calm)
entries.contrast: Emanate takes from: the light emanates from a single bulb.

entries.meaning: To free someone from slavery, legal control, or restriction. ---
examples: The bill would emancipate minors at sixteen.
Lincoln emancipated the slaves in 1863.
She was legally emancipated at seventeen.

entries.meaning: To treat a dead body with chemicals so that it does not decay. ---
examples: Funeral homes embalm most bodies before a viewing.
The Egyptians embalmed their kings.
Lenin's body was embalmed and put on display.
entries.contrast: The l is silent, as in calm and palm: im-BAHM.

entries.meaning: To ban trade in something, or to forbid the release of news until a set time. ---
examples: Several states want to embargo the chemical.
Washington embargoed Cuban sugar in 1960.
The report is embargoed until Monday morning.
entries.contrast: Ends in -o, so the third person adds -es: embargoes, embargoed.

entries.meaning: To display a name, design, or slogan prominently on something. ---
examples: Teams emblazon the sponsor's name across the chest.
They emblazoned the logo on every window.
His face was emblazoned on a million posters.
entries.contrast: Emblazon takes on or with: emblazoned on the door, emblazoned with a crest.

entries.meaning: To be a clear example or physical expression of an idea or quality. ---
examples: Few leaders embody the values they preach.
That building embodied everything wrong with the era.
The rules are embodied in a single statute.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: embodies, embodied, but embodying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To press a raised design or lettering into a surface. ---
examples: They can emboss your initials on the cover.
The printer embossed the invitations in gold.
Each card is embossed with the bank's crest.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ss, so the third person adds -es: embosses.

entries.meaning: To involve someone deeply in an argument or a difficult situation. ---
examples: One careless email can embroil a whole department.
The deal embroiled the firm in a two-year lawsuit.
He is embroiled in a fight with his own party.
entries.contrast: Embroil takes in: embroiled in a scandal.

entries.meaning: To act as the host who introduces the acts or speakers at an event. ---
examples: A local comedian will emcee the awards.
She emceed the benefit two years running.
He has been emceeing weddings since college.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (emcee the show), intransitive (he emcees for a living)
entries.contrast: Spelled out from the letters M.C. (master of ceremonies): emcees, emceed, emceeing.

entries.meaning: To show emotion openly, often in an exaggerated or theatrical way. ---
examples: Some actors emote far too much on camera.
He emoted through the entire second act.
She was emoting for the cameras.
entries.русский: бурно выражать чувства, играть с чувством
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ed and -ing: emoted, emoting.

entries.meaning: To mix two liquids that normally separate, such as oil and water, into one smooth blend. ---
examples: Whisk the oil in slowly to emulsify the dressing.
The sauce emulsified as soon as I added the yolk.
Keep emulsifying until it thickens.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (emulsify the butter), intransitive (the sauce emulsifies)
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y: emulsifies, emulsified, but emulsifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with love or admiration, most often used in the passive. ---
examples: The film tries to enamor the audience with nostalgia.
The city enamored her from the first day.
He is not enamored of the new schedule.
entries.contrast: American spelling enamor, British enamour. It usually appears in the passive with of or with: enamored of the idea.

entries.meaning: To express the essence of something briefly, or to enclose it in a protective shell. ---
examples: One photo can encapsulate an entire war.
Her answer encapsulated the whole problem.
The chips are encapsulated in resin.
entries.русский: кратко выражать, резюмировать; заключать в оболочку

entries.meaning: To cover or enclose something completely in a surrounding material. ---
examples: Builders encase the steel in concrete.
Ice encased every branch by morning.
The engine is encased in a soundproof box.
entries.contrast: Encase takes in: encased in glass. Drop the silent -e before -ing: encasing.

entries.meaning: To form a circle around something or someone. ---
examples: A high wall encircles the old town.
Troops encircled the city within a day.
The lake is encircled by pines.

entries.meaning: To put information into a code or a particular form, as in computing or genetics. ---
examples: The app will encode the file before sending it.
They encoded the message with a simple cipher.
This gene encodes a protein that repairs damage.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: encode → encoding. The opposite is decode.

entries.meaning: To include or cover a wide range of things. ---
examples: The term encompasses far more than software.
The survey encompassed twelve states.
The park was expanded to encompass the wetlands.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ss, so the third person adds -es: encompasses.

entries.meaning: To move gradually into someone else's space, time, or rights. ---
examples: New subdivisions encroach on the forest every year.
Work encroached on every weekend that spring.
The desert has been encroaching for decades.
entries.contrast: Encroach takes on or upon: encroach on his rights. Third person adds -es: encroaches.

entries.meaning: To try hard to do something. ---
examples: We endeavor to answer every message within a day.
She endeavored to keep her voice steady.
They have endeavored to settle the case quietly.
entries.contrast: American spelling endeavor, British endeavour. It takes a to-infinitive: endeavor to explain.

entries.meaning: To drain someone of energy and strength. ---
examples: Long meetings in a hot room enervate even the most patient staff.
The humidity enervated the whole crew by noon.
She found the endless paperwork enervating.
entries.contrast: Enervate means to weaken, not to energize, despite how the word looks.

entries.meaning: To give a group of people the legal right to vote. ---
examples: The amendment would enfranchise residents of the territory.
A 1920 amendment enfranchised women nationwide.
Millions were finally enfranchised after the law passed.
entries.русский: предоставлять избирательное право, наделять правом голоса
entries.contrast: The opposite, disenfranchise, is far more common in the news: disenfranchised voters.

entries.meaning: To cause a feeling or a situation to come into being. ---
examples: Small kindnesses engender loyalty.
The mayor's response engendered real anger.
Years of secrecy had engendered deep distrust.

entries.meaning: To arrange something cleverly or secretly so that it happens. ---
examples: Lobbyists engineer deals like this behind closed doors.
He engineered a trade that saved the team's season.
The takeover was engineered by two board members.
entries.contrast: As a verb it does not mean to work as an engineer; it means to arrange something skillfully.

entries.meaning: To take up all of someone's attention. ---
examples: Puzzles like that engross him for hours.
The novel engrossed her so completely that she missed her stop.
He was engrossed in the game and never heard the doorbell.
entries.contrast: Almost always passive: be engrossed IN something.

entries.meaning: To order someone to do something, or in law to forbid an action by court order. ---
examples: Judges can enjoin a company from selling the product.
The court enjoined the state from enforcing the rule.
The agency has been enjoined twice this year.
entries.contrast: In American legal news it usually means the opposite of order: enjoin someone FROM doing something = forbid it.

entries.meaning: To make something more lively or more interesting. ---
examples: A few good questions enliven any lecture.
Her stories enlivened the long drive.
The old square has been enlivened by new cafes.

entries.meaning: To involve someone deeply in a situation that is hard to get out of. ---
examples: Bad loans can enmesh a family for years.
The scandal enmeshed three senior officials.
He is enmeshed in a lawsuit he never wanted.
entries.contrast: Usually passive: be enmeshed IN something.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something finer in character. ---
examples: Hard work does not automatically ennoble anyone.
The director claimed that suffering had ennobled his hero.
Volunteering there was an ennobling experience for the whole town.

entries.meaning: To settle someone comfortably or securely in a place. ---
examples: Cats ensconce themselves in the warmest spot in the house.
She ensconced herself in the corner booth with a book.
He has been ensconced in that office for twenty years.
entries.contrast: Nearly always reflexive or passive: ensconce yourself somewhere, be ensconced in a place.

entries.meaning: To preserve a right or an idea in a form that protects it permanently. ---
examples: Constitutions enshrine basic freedoms.
The treaty enshrined the right to appeal.
That principle is enshrined in state law.
entries.contrast: Almost always passive: be enshrined IN a law, a constitution, a charter.

entries.meaning: To make someone a slave, or to put someone completely under another's control. ---
examples: Debt can enslave a whole generation.
Colonial powers enslaved millions of people.
Their families had been enslaved for three generations.

entries.meaning: To catch someone or something in a trap, literally or figuratively. ---
examples: Cheap credit offers ensnare young borrowers.
The net ensnared a dolphin along with the tuna.
Two executives were ensnared in the investigation.

entries.meaning: To involve something as a necessary part or result. ---
examples: What exactly does this job entail?
The renovation entailed three months of noise.
The change has entailed a lot of extra paperwork.
entries.русский: влечь за собой, повлечь; требовать, предполагать

entries.meaning: To catch something in a tangle, or to involve someone in a complicated problem. ---
examples: Loose lines entangle propellers every summer.
The whale entangled itself in fishing gear.
He got entangled in a long legal fight.

entries.meaning: To hold someone's attention completely because something is so interesting or beautiful. ---
examples: Street magicians enthrall the tourists on the pier.
Her performance enthralled the whole theater.
The kids sat enthralled through the entire show.
entries.contrast: American English doubles the l: enthrall, enthralled, enthralling. British writing also uses enthral.

entries.meaning: To talk about something with obvious excitement. ---
examples: Fans still enthuse about that album.
She enthused over the new bakery for ten minutes.
He came back enthusing about the hiking trails.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the speech enthused the crowd), intransitive (she enthused about the trip)
entries.contrast: Enthuse ABOUT or OVER something. It is a back-formation from enthusiasm and stays informal.

entries.meaning: To attract someone by offering something appealing. ---
examples: Free shipping entices a lot of shoppers.
The store enticed customers with deep discounts.
He was enticed away by a better offer.
entries.contrast: Entice someone TO do something, or entice them INTO a deal.

entries.meaning: To fill someone with delight and wonder so that they cannot look away. ---
examples: Fireworks still entrance him at forty.
The dancers entranced the whole audience.
The children stood entranced in front of the aquarium.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the noun but stressed differently: the noun ENTRANCE (EN-truhnss) means a way in; the verb is in-TRANSS.

entries.meaning: To trick someone into doing something wrong, especially so they can be caught. ---
examples: Defense lawyers argue that agents entrap their clients.
The sting operation entrapped two dozen buyers.
He claimed he had been entrapped by an undercover officer.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the p doubles: entrapped, entrapping.

entries.meaning: To establish something so firmly that it becomes very hard to change. ---
examples: Tax breaks like these entrench inequality.
The reform entrenched the party's power for a decade.
Corruption is deeply entrenched in the system.
entries.contrast: Most often passive, with deeply: deeply entrenched habits, entrenched interests.

entries.meaning: To twist two or more things together, or to become twisted together. ---
examples: Wisteria vines entwine the porch railing every June.
She entwined her fingers with his.
Their careers have been entwined since college.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (entwine the ribbons), intransitive (the vines entwine)

entries.meaning: To name things on a list one by one. ---
examples: The contract enumerates every possible fee.
She enumerated her objections in order.
The report has enumerated six separate failures.
entries.contrast: No y-sound in American English: i-NOO-muh-rayt, not i-NYOO-muh-rayt.

entries.meaning: To picture something in your mind as a future possibility. ---
examples: We envisage a second location by next spring.
Nobody envisaged a delay this long.
The plan, as originally envisaged, cost half as much.
entries.contrast: Americans more often say envision; envisage is the more formal of the two and belongs to writing.

entries.meaning: To be a perfect example of a quality or a type. ---
examples: Those roadside diners epitomize small-town America.
Her first album epitomized the sound of the decade.
He has epitomized steady leadership for years.
entries.contrast: The noun is epitome, pronounced i-PIT-uh-mee — four syllables, not EP-i-tohm.

entries.meaning: To treat two things as if they were the same. ---
examples: Do not equate silence with agreement.
Critics equated the policy with censorship.
Speed is too often equated with skill.
entries.contrast: Equate one thing WITH another. The related noun is equation.

entries.meaning: To speak vaguely on purpose in order to avoid committing yourself. ---
examples: Politicians equivocate when the polling is bad.
He equivocated for twenty minutes and answered nothing.
She was still equivocating when the hearing ended.
entries.русский: говорить уклончиво, увиливать, уходить от ответа

entries.meaning: To make a mistake. ---
examples: When in doubt, err on the side of caution.
The clerk erred in the company's favor.
Having erred once, he double-checked everything after that.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say it like air; the older pronunciation rhymes with her. The everyday phrase is err ON THE SIDE OF something.

entries.meaning: To get away from a place or a danger. ---
examples: Most drivers escape with nothing worse than a fine.
The family escaped through a back window.
He has escaped serious injury twice this season.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (escape punishment), intransitive (escape from prison)
entries.contrast: Escape FROM a place, but escape a fate with no preposition: escape from jail, escape punishment.

entries.meaning: To deliberately avoid doing or using something. ---
examples: Some chefs eschew salt almost entirely.
The band eschewed studio effects on this record.
She has always eschewed publicity.

entries.meaning: To publicly support a belief or a way of life. ---
examples: Few candidates espouse higher taxes openly.
The paper espoused reform for decades.
The values espoused in that speech were not new.

entries.meaning: To respect and admire someone or something greatly. ---
examples: Colleagues esteem her for her honesty.
Earlier generations esteemed thrift above comfort.
He is widely esteemed as a teacher.
entries.contrast: Usually passive in modern English: a highly esteemed colleague. The noun shows up everywhere in self-esteem.

entries.meaning: To praise someone highly, especially in a speech at their funeral. ---
examples: Old teammates still eulogize him at every reunion.
Her brother eulogized her at the service.
The founder was eulogized in every local paper.
entries.contrast: American English spells it -ize; British writing uses eulogise.

entries.meaning: To end an animal's life painlessly, usually because it is very sick. ---
examples: Shelters euthanize far fewer animals than they used to.
The vet euthanized the old dog that morning.
The horse had to be euthanized after the fall.

entries.meaning: To preach a faith to others, or to promote an idea with the same zeal. ---
examples: Startups hire people to evangelize the product.
He spent ten years evangelizing in rural Brazil.
The method has been evangelized at every conference since.
entries.русский: проповедовать; обращать в веру; активно продвигать (идею)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (evangelize a village), intransitive (they evangelize door to door)

entries.meaning: To show or prove that something is true. ---
examples: These numbers evidence a real shift in demand.
The letters evidenced a long friendship.
Support was strong, as evidenced by the turnout.
entries.contrast: In practice the verb is almost always passive: as evidenced by. The noun is uncountable — much evidence, never evidences.

entries.meaning: To take the heart out of something so that almost nothing useful is left. ---
examples: Budget cuts eviscerate the programs that actually work.
The amendment eviscerated the original bill.
The proposal was eviscerated by outside reviewers.

entries.meaning: To bring a feeling, a memory, or an image into someone's mind. ---
examples: Certain smells evoke childhood instantly.
The photograph evoked a summer she had forgotten.
His music has evoked comparisons to early jazz.

entries.meaning: To make a bad situation worse. ---
examples: Cutting staff now would exacerbate the backlog.
The drought exacerbated the food shortage.
Her injury was exacerbated by playing through it.

entries.meaning: To demand and get something from someone, usually by force or pressure. ---
examples: Storms like this exact a heavy toll on the coast.
The lender exacted a penalty for every late payment.
A high price has been exacted for that silence.
entries.contrast: Same spelling and stress as the adjective exact (precise), but the verb means to demand or impose: exact a toll, exact revenge.

entries.meaning: To praise someone or something very highly, or to raise them to a higher position. ---
examples: Sports writers exalt him every October.
The film exalted ordinary firefighters.
He was exalted to a rank he had not earned.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with exult (ig-ZULT), which means to rejoice. You exalt someone else; you exult yourself.

entries.meaning: To annoy someone very much. ---
examples: Automated phone menus exasperate everyone.
His constant excuses exasperated the whole team.
She was exasperated by one delay after another.

entries.meaning: To dig out earth, especially in order to uncover something buried. ---
examples: Crews excavate the foundation before anything else goes up.
Archaeologists excavated the site in the 1970s.
Only half the tomb has been excavated.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (excavate a site), intransitive (they excavated for three seasons)

entries.meaning: To go beyond a limit or an expectation. ---
examples: Do not exceed the posted speed limit.
Sales exceeded last year's total by March.
The heat has exceeded every previous record.
entries.contrast: Only three common verbs end in -ceed: exceed, proceed, succeed. The rest are -cede (concede, precede).

entries.meaning: To take a short passage out of a longer text for separate use. ---
examples: Magazines often excerpt new memoirs before publication.
The paper excerpted two chapters last Sunday.
The passage was excerpted from her 2019 novel.
entries.contrast: The noun moves the stress to the front: an EK-surpt, but to ik-SURPT a book.

entries.meaning: To cut something out and remove it completely. ---
examples: Editors excise whole paragraphs when space runs short.
The surgeon excised the tumor.
Two scenes were excised before release.
entries.contrast: The tax noun is a different word with front stress: an EK-syz tax. And excise is not exercise.

entries.meaning: To officially exclude someone from a church and its rites. ---
examples: Few churches excommunicate anyone today.
The pope excommunicated him in 1521.
He had been excommunicated years before he died.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone very harshly in public. ---
examples: Editorial boards excoriate the plan every week.
The judge excoriated both attorneys.
He was excoriated in the press for weeks.

entries.meaning: To pass waste matter out of the body or out of a cell. ---
examples: Kidneys excrete most of the drug within a day.
The tree excreted a sticky resin all over the bark.
Salt is excreted through the skin when you sweat.

entries.meaning: To rub away dead cells from the surface of the skin. ---
examples: Dermatologists say you should exfoliate twice a week at most.
She exfoliated before putting on the mask.
Exfoliating too often can leave your skin raw.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exfoliate your skin), intransitive (the rock exfoliates in thin sheets)

entries.meaning: To make someone feel very happy and full of energy. ---
examples: Cold water and open sky exhilarate him.
The first run down the mountain exhilarated her.
We came home tired but exhilarated.
entries.contrast: The h is silent: ig-ZIL-uh-rayt. Note the spelling -hilar-, as in hilarious.

entries.meaning: To urge someone strongly to do something. ---
examples: Coaches exhort their players to finish every drill.
She exhorted the crowd to stay calm.
They were exhorted to give whatever they could.
entries.contrast: The h is silent and the x sounds like gz: ig-ZORT, like exhaust and exhibit.

entries.meaning: To dig up a buried body, usually for an official examination. ---
examples: Courts rarely order officials to exhume a body.
Investigators exhumed the remains in April.
The grave had been exhumed twice before.

entries.meaning: To force someone to leave their own country, usually for political reasons. ---
examples: Regimes still exile their loudest critics.
The junta exiled him in 1976.
He was exiled for writing against the government.
entries.contrast: Both EG-zyl and EK-syl are heard; the noun is spelled and stressed exactly like the verb.

entries.meaning: To be real or present in the world. ---
examples: Does such a thing even exist?
The company existed for less than two years.
Species have existed here for millennia.
entries.contrast: Never takes an object. The noun is existence, spelled -ence, not -ance.

entries.meaning: To drive out an evil spirit, or to get rid of a painful memory. ---
examples: Priests still exorcise houses in some towns.
The trip exorcised a lot of old guilt.
Those ghosts have never really been exorcised.
entries.contrast: Written exorcise or exorcize in the US, and pronounced almost like exercise — but the two words are unrelated.

entries.meaning: To make a process happen faster than usual. ---
examples: For an extra fee they will expedite the passport.
The clerk expedited our paperwork.
Shipping is being expedited for early orders.

entries.meaning: To use up money, time, or energy on something. ---
examples: Do not expend energy on arguments you cannot win.
The city expended most of the grant on repairs.
Half the fuel had been expended before they reached the coast.
entries.contrast: The formal word for spend, with the sense of using something up. The noun is expenditure.

entries.meaning: To feel or live through something. ---
examples: Most travelers experience some jet lag.
The region experienced its worst drought in decades.
Users are experiencing delays this morning.
entries.contrast: Spelled -ience: experience, not experiance.

entries.meaning: To explain an idea in detail. ---
examples: He will expound on that theory for hours.
She expounded her views at the town meeting.
The doctrine is expounded in chapter four.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (expound a theory), intransitive (expound on a topic)
entries.contrast: Expound ON a subject when there is no direct object.

entries.meaning: To take private property away from its owner, especially by government action. ---
examples: States can expropriate land for a highway.
The government expropriated the mines in 1938.
Their farm was expropriated without compensation.

entries.meaning: To remove something completely from a record. ---
examples: Some states let courts expunge juvenile records.
The judge expunged the arrest from his file.
The reference had already been expunged.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: expunging, not expungeing.

entries.meaning: To kill all the members of a group of animals or people. ---
examples: Store-bought poison will not exterminate a termite colony.
Settlers nearly exterminated the bison.
The nest was exterminated last week.

entries.meaning: To praise something very highly. ---
examples: Ads always extol the benefits and skip the risks.
She extolled the virtues of a small kitchen.
The program has been extolled by every reviewer.
entries.contrast: Stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: extolled, extolling. The base spelling extoll is old-fashioned.

entries.meaning: To use known facts to estimate something beyond them. ---
examples: You cannot extrapolate a national trend from one county.
They extrapolated next year's costs from the last three.
The forecast was extrapolated from incomplete data.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (extrapolate a trend), intransitive (extrapolate from the data)
entries.contrast: Extrapolate FROM known data TO a conclusion.

entries.meaning: To give off a quality or a liquid steadily. ---
examples: Good teachers exude calm on the first day of school.
The pine exuded sap all over the hood of the car.
She walked in exuding confidence.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (exude confidence), intransitive (sap exudes from the bark)

entries.meaning: To show great joy, especially after a success. ---
examples: Fans exult whenever that team beats the champions.
He exulted in the victory for a solid week.
The crowd was still exulting an hour later.
entries.contrast: Exult IN or OVER something. Do not confuse it with exalt (ig-ZAWLT), which means to praise.

entries.meaning: To measure or judge something roughly just by looking at it. ---
examples: I never measure the oil — I just eyeball it.
He eyeballed the gap and decided the couch would fit.
She was eyeballing the crowd for a familiar face.
entries.русский: прикидывать на глаз, оценивать на глазок
entries.contrast: Informal. It means to estimate by eye, or simply to stare hard at someone.

entries.meaning: To deal with something difficult, or to be turned toward something. ---
examples: They face a tough decision this week.
The company faced three lawsuits at once.
Our apartment is facing the courtyard, so it stays quiet.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (face a decision), intransitive (the house faces south)
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: facing. Face a problem takes no preposition, but face UP TO a problem is a separate, phrasal meaning.

entries.meaning: To make something false look real, or to pretend. ---
examples: Some students try to fake a doctor's note.
He faked an injury to get out of practice.
The documents had been faked by a former clerk.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fake a signature), intransitive (he was only faking)
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: faking, not fakeing.

entries.meaning: To change information dishonestly so that it is no longer true. ---
examples: Auditors check whether managers falsify the numbers.
He falsified his timesheets for months.
The records had been falsified before the inspection.
entries.contrast: The -y follows a consonant, so it changes: falsifies, falsified — but falsifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To move air onto something, or to make a fire or a strong feeling grow. ---
examples: Dry winds fan the wildfires every August.
She fanned herself with a folded magazine.
His speech was fanning the anger of the crowd.
entries.contrast: Doubles the n before an ending: fanned, fanning.

entries.meaning: To imagine something, especially to think of yourself as being something. ---
examples: He fancies himself a serious chef.
She fancied that someone was following her.
Don't go fancying yourself an expert after one weekend class.
entries.contrast: The y becomes ie in fancies and fancied, but stays in fancying.

entries.meaning: To imagine pleasant things that are unlikely to happen. ---
examples: Kids often fantasize about being famous.
He fantasized that the letter would bring good news.
She spent the whole meeting fantasizing about her vacation.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he fantasized that he had won), intransitive (they fantasize about retiring)
entries.contrast: American spelling is -ize; British books write fantasise.

entries.meaning: To do well or badly in a particular situation. ---
examples: How did you fare on the final exam?
Small farms fared badly during the drought.
The team is faring better than anyone expected.
entries.contrast: Sounds like fair, and looks like the noun fare (the money you pay for a ride).

entries.meaning: To make or shape something by hand, often out of whatever is available. ---
examples: The villagers fashion tools out of scrap metal.
He fashioned a splint from two sticks and a belt.
She was fashioning a costume out of old curtains.

entries.meaning: To become the father of a child, or to create something entirely new. ---
examples: He fathered three children before he turned thirty.
Men who father children very young often finish school late.
Fathering a child at fifty-five surprised everyone who knew him.
entries.русский: становиться отцом, стать отцом; порождать, породить

entries.meaning: To understand something puzzling after thinking hard about it. ---
examples: I can't fathom why she quit such a good job.
Nobody ever fathomed how the thieves got past the alarm.
The full scale of the damage still hasn't been fathomed.
entries.contrast: Almost always negative: can't fathom, couldn't fathom.

entries.meaning: To make someone very tired, or to weaken a material by stressing it again and again. ---
examples: Twelve-hour shifts fatigue even the youngest nurses.
The climb fatigued us far more than we expected.
Years of vibration had fatigued the metal until it cracked.
entries.contrast: The silent -ue drops before -ing: fatigued but fatiguing.

entries.meaning: To praise someone powerful far too much in order to win their favor. ---
examples: Junior staff fawn over the new director.
The waiters fawned on the celebrity all evening.
Reporters were fawning over him before he had said a word.
entries.contrast: Takes over or on: fawn over the boss.

entries.meaning: To disturb someone's calm or shake their confidence. ---
examples: Nothing seems to faze him.
The boos never fazed the kicker.
She was not fazed by the criticism.
entries.contrast: A homophone of phase: faze means to unsettle, a phase is a stage.

entries.meaning: To pretend to have a feeling, an illness or a reaction that you do not really have. ---
examples: Don't feign surprise — you knew about it already.
He feigned illness to get out of the test.
She listened, feigning interest in every word.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: FAYN, exactly like the word fain.

entries.meaning: To make a pretended move in one direction in order to mislead an opponent. ---
examples: Good boxers feint before they throw the real punch.
He feinted left and drove to the basket.
She kept feinting to pull the defender out of position.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like faint (to pass out), but it is a different word.

entries.meaning: To become infected, or, of a bad feeling or problem, to grow worse because nobody deals with it. ---
examples: Untreated cuts can fester quickly in hot weather.
Resentment festered for years before anyone spoke up.
The dispute has been festering since spring.

entries.meaning: To decorate something by hanging chains of flowers, lights or ribbons on it. ---
examples: Volunteers festoon the square with lights every December.
They festooned the hall with paper flowers.
The porch was festooned with banners and streamers.
entries.contrast: Usually festooned with something.

entries.meaning: To tell a small, harmless lie. ---
examples: Kids fib about brushing their teeth.
He fibbed about his age on the application.
Stop fibbing and tell me what really happened.
entries.contrast: Doubles the b: fibbed, fibbing.

entries.meaning: To turn real events into a story by inventing parts of them. ---
examples: The movie fictionalizes the trial for dramatic effect.
He fictionalized his grandmother's escape in his first novel.
The series is a heavily fictionalized account of the war.
entries.contrast: American spelling is -ize; British books write fictionalise.

entries.meaning: To keep making small restless movements because you are bored or nervous. ---
examples: Try not to fidget during the interview.
The kids fidgeted through the whole ceremony.
He kept fidgeting with his sleeve while he waited.
entries.contrast: One t in American spelling: fidgeted, fidgeting.

entries.meaning: To think or conclude something after weighing it up. ---
examples: I figure we'll be there by six.
She figured the repair would cost a fortune.
Figuring she was already asleep, he let himself in quietly.
entries.contrast: Different from the phrasal verb figure out, which means to solve or understand.

entries.meaning: To get something by clever or slightly dishonest means. ---
examples: He can finagle a table at any restaurant in town.
She finagled an upgrade to first class.
They spent the afternoon finagling their way backstage.

entries.meaning: To make small careful adjustments so that something works as well as possible. ---
examples: We still need to fine-tune the schedule.
They fine-tuned the engine the night before the race.
The team has been fine-tuning the app all week.
entries.contrast: Written with a hyphen: fine-tune, fine-tuned.

entries.meaning: To handle a difficult situation with skill, often by quietly getting around the hard part. ---
examples: A good manager can finesse a question like that.
She finessed the budget problem without firing anyone.
They are still finessing the wording of the deal.

entries.meaning: To attack a building or vehicle with a bomb that sets it on fire. ---
examples: Extremists threatened to firebomb the warehouse.
Someone firebombed the campaign office overnight.
Three cars were firebombed on the same street last month.

entries.meaning: Of a vehicle, to slide from side to side at the back because the rear wheels lose grip. ---
examples: Light trucks fishtail easily on wet roads.
The trailer fishtailed and nearly flipped.
He felt the car fishtailing on the ice and let off the gas.

entries.meaning: To think about one thing so much that you cannot think about anything else. ---
examples: Don't fixate on one bad review.
He fixated on a single detail of her story.
The press keeps fixating on the candidate's age.
entries.contrast: Takes on: fixate on something.

entries.meaning: To produce a lot of small bubbles with a soft hissing sound. ---
examples: The tablet fizzes as soon as it hits the water.
The soda fizzed over the rim of the glass.
The champagne was still fizzing when we raised our glasses.
entries.contrast: Adds -es in the third person: fizzes.

entries.meaning: To begin with promise and then fail or fade away weakly. ---
examples: Most of these campaigns fizzle after a week.
The rally fizzled in the rain.
Their romance was already fizzling by June.
entries.contrast: Often with out, as in the phrasal verb fizzle out, with the same meaning.

entries.meaning: To astonish someone so much that they can hardly speak. ---
examples: The repair bill will flabbergast you.
The verdict flabbergasted everyone in the courtroom.
We were flabbergasted by how cheap the tickets were.
entries.contrast: Most often passive: be flabbergasted by something.

entries.meaning: To wave your arms or legs about wildly, or to struggle with no control. ---
examples: Don't flail your arms — just float.
He flailed in the deep end until a lifeguard reached him.
The company has been flailing since the recall.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't flail your arms), intransitive (he flailed in the water)

entries.meaning: To be or move at the side of someone or something. ---
examples: Two stone lions flank the entrance.
Bodyguards flanked the senator as she left the building.
He arrived flanked by his lawyers.
entries.русский: располагаться по бокам; окружать с флангов

entries.meaning: To stop showing any activity or growth, whether a heartbeat on a monitor or a set of numbers. ---
examples: Wages flatline whenever hiring slows down.
The patient flatlined twice on the operating table.
Sales have been flatlining since January.

entries.meaning: To charge someone far too much, or to cheat them out of their money. ---
examples: Some shops near the airport fleece tourists.
The contractor fleeced them for thousands of dollars.
Elderly customers were being fleeced by phone scammers.

entries.meaning: To move something with a quick, light movement of a finger or wrist. ---
examples: Flick the switch on your way out.
She flicked a crumb off the table.
He was flicking water at his little brother.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (flick the switch), intransitive (her eyes flicked to the door)

entries.meaning: To switch to the opposite opinion or position, especially in politics. ---
examples: Candidates who flip-flop lose credibility fast.
The mayor flip-flopped on the tax within a week.
He's been flip-flopping about the job offer for days.
entries.русский: менять позицию на противоположную; идти на попятную
entries.contrast: Doubles the p: flip-flopped, flip-flopping. The noun flip-flop is also a rubber sandal.

entries.meaning: To move quickly and lightly from one place to another. ---
examples: Hummingbirds flit from flower to flower.
She flitted between three conversations at the party.
A shadow kept flitting across the wall.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: flitted, flitting.

entries.meaning: To beat someone hard with a whip or a stick as a punishment. ---
examples: In those days the navy would flog deserters.
The prisoner was flogged in the public square.
Stop flogging that dead horse — the decision is final.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: flogged, flogging.

entries.meaning: To drop down heavily, or, of a movie or product, to fail completely. ---
examples: After work I just flop onto the couch.
The movie flopped at the box office.
The fish was still flopping around in the bucket.
entries.contrast: Doubles the p: flopped, flopping.

entries.meaning: To clean between your teeth with a thin waxed thread. ---
examples: You should floss before you brush.
He flossed for the first time in a year.
Flossing takes less than a minute.
entries.русский: чистить зубной нитью, почистить зубной нитью
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (floss your teeth), intransitive (floss twice a day)

entries.meaning: To struggle helplessly, either in water or in a difficult situation. ---
examples: New teachers often flounder in their first year.
He floundered through the interview and forgot half his answers.
The company has been floundering since the recall.
entries.contrast: Not the same as founder: to flounder is to struggle, to founder is to sink or fail outright.

entries.meaning: To break a rule or law openly and without shame. ---
examples: Drivers flout the speed limit on this stretch of road.
The company flouted safety rules for years.
They were fined for openly flouting the ban.
entries.contrast: Not flaunt: you flout a rule but flaunt your wealth.

entries.meaning: To do something clumsily or to make an embarrassing mistake. ---
examples: Don't flub the punch line this time.
He flubbed his lines in the very first scene.
She has already flubbed two easy shots.
entries.contrast: Doubles the b: flubbed, flubbing.

entries.meaning: To shake or pat something so that it becomes softer and fuller. ---
examples: Fluff the rice with a fork before serving.
She fluffed the pillows and straightened the quilt.
The bird sat on the wire fluffing its feathers.

entries.meaning: To make someone so nervous and confused that they cannot think clearly. ---
examples: Big crowds fluster him.
The lawyer's question flustered the witness.
He got flustered and forgot his own address.
entries.contrast: Usually passive: get flustered, be flustered.

entries.meaning: To force something unwanted on someone. ---
examples: Don't foist your chores on your sister.
They foisted a useless warranty on every buyer.
New rules are being foisted on schools with no warning.
entries.contrast: Takes on or upon: foist something on someone.

entries.meaning: To deliberately stir up trouble, anger or unrest. ---
examples: Those broadcasts foment hatred between neighbors.
The article fomented days of protest.
He was accused of fomenting a rebellion.

entries.meaning: To stroke or handle someone or something gently and lovingly. ---
examples: He would fondle the dog's ears while he read.
She fondled the fabric before deciding to buy it.
He sat fondling the old coin in his pocket.
entries.contrast: With a person as the object it usually suggests unwanted sexual touching, so use it carefully.

entries.meaning: To cross a river or stream at a shallow place, on foot or by vehicle. ---
examples: We had to ford the creek to reach the trailhead.
The wagons forded the river at dawn.
Fording the stream in spring can be dangerous.

entries.meaning: To be an early sign of something that will happen later. ---
examples: The opening scene foreshadows the ending.
Falling orders foreshadowed the layoffs.
The storm was foreshadowed by an eerie stillness.

entries.meaning: To warn someone about something before it happens. ---
examples: I should forewarn you — the main road is closed.
The city forewarned residents about the water shutoff.
We had been forewarned about the traffic.

entries.meaning: Of a road, river or path, to divide into two branches. ---
examples: The trail forks just past the bridge.
The river forked around a small island.
Stay to the right after the road has forked.

entries.meaning: To make an arrangement official by putting it into fixed, written form. ---
examples: We should formalize the agreement in writing.
The two schools formalized their partnership last year.
They are still formalizing the details of the merger.
entries.contrast: American spelling is -ize; British books write formalise.

entries.meaning: To work out a plan, policy or idea and put it into clear words. ---
examples: It takes weeks to formulate a good research question.
The committee formulated a new safety policy.
She is still formulating her answer.

entries.meaning: To fail completely, or, of a ship, to fill with water and sink. ---
examples: Talks between the two sides began to founder almost at once.
The startup foundered after its main investor pulled out.
Three fishing boats had foundered in the storm.
entries.русский: терпеть неудачу, потерпеть крах; идти ко дну, затонуть
entries.contrast: Founder (fail, sink) is not flounder (struggle clumsily): a company that founders has already gone under, one that flounders is still thrashing about.

entries.meaning: To pump liquid into rock at high pressure in order to release the oil or gas trapped inside. ---
examples: Several states refuse to let companies frack near reservoirs.
They fracked the same well twice last year.
Thousands of wells have been fracked across the state.
entries.русский: проводить гидроразрыв пласта, добывать методом гидроразрыва
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (frack a well), intransitive (the company has been fracking here since 2010)

entries.meaning: To break into small separate pieces, or to break something apart in that way. ---
examples: Too many small parties fragment the vote.
The opposition fragmented into half a dozen groups.
The audience has fragmented since streaming arrived.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the war fragmented the country), intransitive (the coalition fragmented)

entries.meaning: To let someone run a business under your company's name and system in return for a fee. ---
examples: The chain plans to franchise its stores overseas.
They franchised the brand in forty countries.
Most of the restaurants are franchised, not company-owned.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: franchising, not franchiseing.

entries.meaning: To mix socially with people you are supposed to keep your distance from. ---
examples: Officers are told not to fraternize with the enlisted ranks.
He was disciplined for fraternizing with a supplier.
Guards who fraternized with inmates lost their jobs.
entries.contrast: Always fraternize with someone. American English spells it -ize; British English uses fraternise.

entries.meaning: To wear someone out completely, leaving them tired and on edge. ---
examples: Two hours in traffic can frazzle anyone.
The long flight frazzled the whole family.
She looked frazzled after a week of night shifts.

entries.meaning: To work for several clients job by job rather than for one employer. ---
examples: She wants to freelance for a year before taking a staff job.
He freelanced as a translator while he was studying.
They have been freelancing since the magazine closed.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: freelancing.

entries.meaning: To live off other people's money, food, or hospitality without giving anything back. ---
examples: He is happy to freeload as long as somebody lets him.
They freeloaded off her parents all summer.
She accused her roommate of freeloading.
entries.русский: жить за чужой счёт, нахлебничать, паразитировать
entries.contrast: Freeload off (or on) someone.

entries.meaning: To load something with cargo, or to load a word or act with meaning and feeling. ---
examples: The company freights grain down the river.
They freighted the train with coal and timber.
The word is freighted with a century of history.
entries.contrast: Freight rhymes with eight — the -gh- is silent.

entries.meaning: To go to a place often. ---
examples: Students frequent the cafés around campus.
He frequented the same diner for twenty years.
The bar is frequented by off-duty police.
entries.contrast: The verb moves the stress: the adjective is FREE-kwuhnt, the verb is fri-KWENT.

entries.meaning: To add someone to your list of contacts on a social network. ---
examples: Go ahead and friend me on the app.
She friended three old classmates last night.
He has friended almost everyone from high school.
entries.русский: добавлять в друзья, добавить в друзья
entries.contrast: The opposite is unfriend, not defriend, in ordinary American usage.

entries.meaning: To curl into small tight curls, or to make hair do that. ---
examples: Humidity makes fine hair frizz within minutes.
The blow dryer frizzed her curls.
Her hair had frizzed into a halo by noon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the dryer frizzed her hair), intransitive (my hair frizzes in humid weather)
entries.contrast: Verbs ending in -zz take -es in the third person: frizz → frizzes.

entries.meaning: To play and move about in a lively, carefree way. ---
examples: The lambs frolic in the field all morning.
The kids frolicked in the sprinkler until dinner.
Two otters were frolicking in the shallows.
entries.contrast: Add a k before -ed and -ing, as in panic: frolicked, frolicking — never frolicing.

entries.meaning: To produce a mass of small bubbles, or to whip something until it does. ---
examples: Heat the milk, then froth it for the latte.
The wave frothed white against the rocks.
He was frothing with rage by the end of the call.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (froth the milk), intransitive (the beer frothed over the rim)

entries.meaning: To present something in a deliberately vague or dishonest way so that a problem stays hidden. ---
examples: Don't fudge the deadline — tell them the truth.
The lab fudged its results for two years.
The wording had been fudged to satisfy both sides.
entries.русский: подтасовывать, подтасовать; уходить от прямого ответа
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fudge the numbers), intransitive (he fudged when we asked)
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: fudging.

entries.meaning: To supply something with fuel, or to make a feeling or process grow stronger. ---
examples: Cheap credit can fuel a housing boom.
The rumors fueled the panic.
The plane was being fueled on the tarmac.
entries.contrast: American English writes fueled and fueling with one l; British English doubles it: fuelled, fuelling.

entries.meaning: To attack something loudly and angrily in speech or in print. ---
examples: Columnists fulminate about the new tax every week.
He fulminated against the decision for a full hour.
She has been fulminating on the subject for years.
entries.русский: метать громы и молнии, гневно обличать
entries.contrast: Fulminate against something.

entries.meaning: To be visibly angry, often without saying much about it. ---
examples: Passengers fume while the gate agent says nothing.
He fumed all the way home.
She was still fuming about the comment a week later.
entries.русский: злиться, кипеть от злости; дымить, испускать пары

entries.meaning: To fill a place with chemical smoke or gas in order to kill insects or germs. ---
examples: They have to fumigate the greenhouse twice a year.
The landlord fumigated the apartment for bedbugs.
The building had been fumigated the week before.

entries.meaning: To work or operate in the way something is supposed to. ---
examples: The heater doesn't function below freezing.
The old system functioned well enough for years.
The clinic has been functioning without a doctor since May.
entries.contrast: Function as something: the sofa functions as a spare bed.

entries.meaning: To make deep lines or grooves in something, especially in your forehead. ---
examples: He tends to furrow his brow when he reads.
She furrowed her forehead at the question.
His face was furrowed with worry.

entries.meaning: To join two things into one, especially by heat, or to become joined in that way. ---
examples: The technique fuses glass and metal.
The cracked vertebrae fused on their own.
The band has fused jazz with hip-hop.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heat fuses the two metals), intransitive (the broken bones fused)
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: fusing.

entries.meaning: To choke or retch, or to stop someone from speaking freely. ---
examples: Some people gag every time they swallow a pill.
The court order gagged the newspaper for a month.
He was gagging on the smoke before he reached the door.
entries.русский: давиться, тошнить; затыкать рот, заставлять молчать
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the order gagged the newspaper), intransitive (he gagged on the pill)
entries.contrast: One vowel + one final consonant doubles: gag → gagged, gagging.

entries.meaning: To annoy or humiliate someone deeply. ---
examples: It galls me that nobody has apologized.
The decision galled everyone on the team.
He was galled at being passed over again.

entries.meaning: To travel around enjoying yourself instead of doing what you should be doing. ---
examples: They gallivant all over Europe every summer.
He gallivanted around town while his brother worked.
She has been gallivanting ever since she retired.

entries.meaning: To manipulate a system or a set of rules in order to get an unfair advantage. ---
examples: Sellers try to game the review rankings.
They gamed the tax code for years.
The algorithm turned out to be easily gamed.
entries.русский: манипулировать (системой), обходить правила в свою пользу
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: gaming.

entries.meaning: To stare with your mouth open in surprise, or, of a hole, to lie wide open. ---
examples: Tourists stop on the steps and gape at the ceiling.
She gaped at him in disbelief.
A hole was gaping in the roof where the tree fell.
entries.contrast: Gape at someone or something.

entries.meaning: To repeat or transmit a message so badly that it no longer makes sense. ---
examples: Bad reception can garble a whole call.
The clerk garbled the address.
The radio message came through garbled.

entries.meaning: To collect or earn something, especially support, praise, or attention. ---
examples: The bill will garner very few votes.
The film garnered six nominations.
She has garnered a large following online.
entries.contrast: Garner (collect, win) is not garnish (decorate a dish, or take money out of wages).

entries.meaning: To attack, injure, or kill someone with poisonous gas. ---
examples: Riot police threatened to gas the crowd.
Artillery gassed the trenches before dawn.
Hundreds had been gassed by the time the wind shifted.
entries.contrast: The s doubles all the way through the verb: gasses, gassed, gassing — but the plural of the noun is gases.

entries.meaning: To cut a long, deep wound in something. ---
examples: A loose nail can gash your hand.
He gashed his knee on the rocks.
Her arm was badly gashed in the fall.
entries.contrast: Verbs ending in -sh take -es in the third person: gash → gashes.

entries.meaning: To manipulate someone into doubting their own memory, judgment, or sanity. ---
examples: Don't let anyone gaslight you about what you saw.
He gaslighted her for years before she left.
She slowly realized she was being gaslighted.
entries.contrast: The verb is regular: gaslighted, not gaslit — gaslit describes a street lit by gas lamps.

entries.meaning: To judge or measure the size, amount, or strength of something. ---
examples: It's hard to gauge how angry she really is.
We gauged interest with a short survey.
Support has been gauged by three separate polls.
entries.contrast: Spelled gauge but pronounced GAYJ; the silent -e drops before -ing: gauging.

entries.meaning: To stare at something rudely or stupidly. ---
examples: Drivers slow down to gawk at the wreck.
The kids gawked at the size of the fish.
Stop gawking and give me a hand.
entries.contrast: Gawk at something.

entries.meaning: To come together into something that works well, or to set into a thick, jelly-like form. ---
examples: It takes a season for a new team to gel.
The plan finally gelled over dinner.
The mixture is gelling nicely in the fridge.
entries.contrast: Double the l: gel → gelled, gelling. American English also spells the same verb jell.

entries.meaning: To go down on one knee in worship or respect, or to show someone exaggerated deference. ---
examples: Worshippers genuflect before entering the pew.
He genuflected quickly at the altar.
The party has spent years genuflecting to its donors.
entries.contrast: Genuflect to or before someone.

entries.meaning: To redraw the boundaries of voting districts so that one party wins more seats than its share of the vote. ---
examples: Both parties gerrymander when they get the chance.
The legislature gerrymandered the map right after the census.
The district had been gerrymandered beyond recognition.
entries.contrast: The g is soft: JER-ee-man-dur, not GER-.

entries.meaning: To make lively movements with your hands and arms while speaking. ---
examples: He tends to gesticulate when he gets excited.
She gesticulated toward the far end of the room.
Two men were gesticulating at each other across the street.

entries.meaning: To end a relationship by suddenly cutting off all contact and giving no explanation. ---
examples: People ghost each other constantly on dating apps.
He ghosted her after three dates.
She has been ghosted by two employers this year.
entries.русский: внезапно обрывать общение, пропадать без объяснений

entries.meaning: To make someone feel happy or pleased. ---
examples: Small kindnesses gladden the heart.
The news gladdened everyone at the table.
She was gladdened by how many people came.

entries.meaning: To make something look more attractive or exciting than it really is. ---
examples: These films glamorize street crime.
The old ads glamorized smoking.
War is too often glamorized on screen.
entries.contrast: American English spells it glamorize; British English uses glamorise or glamourise.

entries.meaning: To collect information or facts slowly, a little at a time. ---
examples: You can glean a lot from the footnotes.
Investigators gleaned the details from old emails.
Very little has been gleaned from the recording.
entries.contrast: Glean something from a source.

entries.meaning: To give off small, quick flashes of reflected light. ---
examples: Broken glass glints on the pavement.
The knife glinted in the lamplight.
Something was glinting at the bottom of the pool.

entries.meaning: To show open, selfish pleasure at your own success or at someone else's misfortune. ---
examples: Win if you can, but don't gloat.
He gloated about the result all week.
They were still gloating over the verdict on Monday.
entries.contrast: Gloat over or about something.

entries.meaning: To spread a business, market, or practice across the whole world. ---
examples: Cheap shipping helped globalize manufacturing.
The firm globalized its supply chain in the 1990s.
Fashion has been thoroughly globalized.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (globalize production), intransitive (the industry globalized fast)
entries.contrast: American English spells it -ize; British English uses globalise.

entries.meaning: To praise something, or to make it seem far better or more important than it is. ---
examples: The song seems to glorify violence.
Old textbooks glorified the conquest.
It's a glorified shed, nothing more.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y becomes -ies and -ied: glorifies, glorified — but -ing keeps the y: glorifying.

entries.meaning: To look at someone with an angry, sullen expression. ---
examples: He glowers whenever the subject comes up.
The bouncer glowered at us from the door.
She sat glowering in the corner all evening.
entries.contrast: Glower rhymes with power, not with lower; you glower at someone.

entries.meaning: To supply far more of something than the market can absorb. ---
examples: Cheap imports glut the market every spring.
New drilling glutted the world with oil.
The shelves were glutted with unsold copies.
entries.contrast: One vowel + one final consonant doubles: glut → glutted, glutting.

entries.meaning: To grind your teeth together in anger or distress. ---
examples: Losing candidates gnash their teeth and blame the weather.
He gnashed his teeth when he heard the number.
There was a lot of gnashing of teeth in the newsroom.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: NASH. Third person adds -es: gnashes.

entries.meaning: To provoke someone into doing something, usually something unwise. ---
examples: Don't let them goad you into answering.
His brother goaded him into the fight.
She had been goaded all evening before she snapped.
entries.contrast: Goad someone into doing something.

entries.meaning: To eat something quickly and greedily. ---
examples: The kids gobble anything you put on the table.
He gobbled his sandwich in the car.
The dog had gobbled the whole bag before we noticed.

entries.meaning: To make a careless mistake, or to waste time instead of working. ---
examples: I goofed — I sent it to the wrong address.
They were goofing around in the parking lot.
He has goofed off all week.
entries.transitivity: intransitive — usually with up, off, or around
entries.contrast: Informal. The particle changes the meaning completely: goof up is to make a mistake, goof off is to shirk work, and goof around is to fool about harmlessly. The noun a goof is both the mistake and the person who makes it.

entries.meaning: To wound someone by driving a horn or tusk into them. ---
examples: A bull can gore a man in seconds.
The elephant gored two of the guides.
He was gored during the run in Pamplona.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: goring.

entries.meaning: To eat a very large amount of something, usually more than is good for you. ---
examples: Bears gorge on salmon before winter.
We gorged ourselves at the buffet.
The kids had been gorging on candy all afternoon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (gorge yourself on cake), intransitive (the bears gorge before winter)
entries.contrast: Gorge (yourself) on something.

entries.meaning: To make a place or an occasion more attractive or more important by being there. ---
examples: Few stars grace a festival this small.
Her portrait graced the cover of the program.
The hall has been graced by three presidents.
entries.contrast: Drop the silent -e before -ing: gracing.

entries.meaning: To behave in a showy way in order to impress an audience. ---
examples: Senators grandstand whenever the cameras are on.
He grandstanded through the whole hearing.
She accused her opponent of grandstanding.

entries.meaning: To please or satisfy someone, or to satisfy a desire. ---
examples: It would gratify her to hear you say that.
The response gratified the whole staff.
We were gratified by the turnout.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y becomes -ies and -ied: gratifies, gratified — but -ing keeps the y: gratifying.

entries.meaning: To be drawn steadily toward a person, a place, or a kind of thing. ---
examples: Students gravitate toward the cheapest housing.
He gravitated to the back of the room.
Buyers have gravitated toward smaller cars.
entries.contrast: Gravitate toward or to something.

entries.meaning: To turn gray, especially of hair, or to make something gray. ---
examples: Most people start to gray in their forties.
Ten years of night shifts grayed his hair.
The country's population is graying fast.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (worry grayed his hair), intransitive (he is graying at the temples)
entries.contrast: American English spells it gray, grayed, graying; British English uses grey, greyed, greying.

entries.meaning: To give official approval for a project to go ahead. ---
examples: The board will greenlight the budget on Friday.
The studio greenlighted a second season.
Two of the films have been greenlighted already.
entries.contrast: Regular in careful writing — greenlighted — though greenlit is common in entertainment news.

entries.meaning: To make money by cheating people, usually with a convincing story. ---
examples: Con artists grift the elderly by phone every single day.
He grifted thousands of dollars out of his own supporters.
She realized the coach had been grifting the whole time.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (grifted his own fans), intransitive (he has been grifting for years)

entries.meaning: To twist your face for a moment because of pain, disgust, or annoyance. ---
examples: Try not to grimace when you taste it.
He grimaced and grabbed his knee.
She was grimacing through the last mile of the race.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the first syllable in American English: GRIM-uhs, not gri-MAYS.

entries.meaning: To complain in a steady, low-level, annoying way about small things. ---
examples: The players gripe about the practice schedule every year.
He griped that the coffee was cold again.
They spent the whole drive griping about traffic.
entries.contrast: You gripe about something; drop the -e before -ing: griping, not gripeing.

entries.meaning: To press your teeth tightly together, usually to get through pain or anger. ---
examples: Grit your teeth — this will only take a second.
He gritted his teeth and kept walking on the broken ankle.
She answered politely, gritting her teeth the whole time.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: gritted, gritting.

entries.meaning: To feel around with your hands because you cannot see, or to touch someone sexually without their consent. ---
examples: I had to grope for the light switch in the dark hallway.
He groped his way down the basement stairs.
The witness said she was groping for the right word.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (groped the wall for a switch), intransitive (groped in the dark)

entries.meaning: To earn a total amount of money before taxes and expenses are taken out. ---
examples: Sequels like this usually gross more overseas than at home.
The film grossed two hundred million dollars in three weeks.
The tour has grossed more than any other this year.
entries.contrast: Gross out (to disgust) is a separate phrasal verb: that video grossed me out.

entries.meaning: To make a short, low sound in your throat, often instead of speaking. ---
examples: Teenagers sometimes just grunt instead of answering.
He grunted something and went back to his phone.
The weightlifter was grunting with every rep.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (grunted an answer), intransitive (the pig grunted)

entries.meaning: To laugh loudly and coarsely. ---
examples: Half the room will guffaw at that joke.
The audience guffawed at the senator's answer.
They were still guffawing when the lights came up.

entries.meaning: To execute someone by cutting off their head with a guillotine. ---
examples: The revolutionaries would guillotine anyone they called an enemy.
They guillotined the king in January 1793.
Thousands had been guillotined by the end of the Terror.
entries.contrast: The gu- is a hard g and the -ll- is a plain l: GIL-uh-teen.

entries.meaning: To pressure someone into doing something by making them feel guilty. ---
examples: Don't let them guilt you into working the weekend.
She guilted her brother into driving her to the airport.
I'm tired of being guilted into covering other people's shifts.
entries.русский: давить на совесть, заставлять чувством вины; пристыдить
entries.contrast: Almost always with into: guilt someone into doing something.

entries.meaning: To make a low bubbling sound, like water running through a narrow pipe. ---
examples: The radiators gurgle whenever the heat comes on.
The stream gurgled over the rocks behind the cabin.
The baby lay in her crib gurgling happily.

entries.meaning: To take the insides out of a fish or animal, or to destroy the inside of a building or the substance of a law. ---
examples: You have to gut and clean the fish before you freeze it.
The fire gutted three floors of the warehouse.
The bill was gutted in committee.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: gutted, gutting.

entries.meaning: To drink or consume something quickly and greedily. ---
examples: Those old trucks guzzle gas.
He guzzled the whole bottle of water in one go.
The air conditioner has been guzzling electricity all summer.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (guzzle a liter of soda), intransitive (he sat there guzzling)

entries.meaning: To turn or swing around in fast circles. ---
examples: The dancers gyrate under the strobe lights.
The helicopter blades gyrated slowly to a stop.
Stock prices have been gyrating all week.
entries.contrast: The g sounds like j: JY-rayt, not GY-rayt.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something get used to a situation, so that it stops feeling strange. ---
examples: Short daily sessions habituate the dog to the crate.
Years abroad had habituated her to the cold.
The birds quickly became habituated to people.
entries.contrast: Usually habituate someone to something.

entries.meaning: To see or hear things that are not really there. ---
examples: High fevers can make small children hallucinate.
He hallucinated for two days after the surgery.
The model had hallucinated three citations that do not exist.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the chatbot hallucinated a source), intransitive (the patient was hallucinating)

entries.meaning: To cut something into two equal parts, or to reduce it to half its size. ---
examples: Halve the potatoes before you roast them.
The company halved its workforce in a single year.
Emissions have been halved since 2005.
entries.русский: делить пополам, разделить пополам; сокращать вдвое
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (halve the recipe), intransitive (sales halved)
entries.contrast: The l is silent — halve sounds exactly like have: HAV.

entries.meaning: To put someone at a disadvantage. ---
examples: Late funding will handicap the whole project.
Poor eyesight handicapped him for years.
Small farms are handicapped by the new labeling rules.
entries.русский: ставить в невыгодное положение, затруднять; мешать
entries.contrast: Doubles the p even though the stress is on the first syllable: handicapped, handicapping.

entries.meaning: To choose someone or something personally and with great care. ---
examples: The founders handpick every new hire.
She handpicked the four people on her team.
The panel was handpicked by the governor's office.
entries.contrast: Also written hand-pick; both spellings are common in American English.

entries.meaning: To take place, especially without being planned. ---
examples: Things like that happen all the time around here.
Nobody could explain what happened that night.
It has happened twice this month already.
entries.contrast: Happen is never passive: say what happened?, never what was happened?

entries.meaning: To speak to someone at length in an angry, scolding way. ---
examples: He likes to harangue callers who disagree with him.
The coach harangued the team for twenty minutes.
She was haranguing shoppers from the sidewalk.
entries.contrast: The final -ue is silent: huh-RANG; it drops before -ing — haranguing.

entries.meaning: To build something in permanently, either into a machine's circuits or into someone's nature. ---
examples: Engineers hardwire the limit so that no one can change it later.
They hardwired the alarm into the building's power supply.
Humans seem to be hardwired to notice faces.
entries.русский: жёстко встраивать, встроить; запрограммировать (в схему или в природу)
entries.contrast: Also written hard-wire; the figurative sense is nearly always passive: we're hardwired to...

entries.meaning: To make something happen sooner, or to hurry to say or do something. ---
examples: Cutting rates now could hasten a recovery.
The scandal hastened his resignation.
She hastened to add that nothing had been decided.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hasten the collapse), intransitive (I hasten to add)
entries.contrast: The t is silent: HAY-suhn.

entries.meaning: To sell goods aggressively, often on the street or door to door. ---
examples: Vendors hawk bottled water outside the stadium.
He hawked cheap watches on the boardwalk all summer.
They have been hawking the same diet pills for years.

entries.meaning: To offer a guess or an opinion even though you might well be wrong. ---
examples: I'd hazard a guess that half of them never read it.
She hazarded an opinion and was immediately shouted down.
No one has hazarded a firm estimate yet.

entries.meaning: To force new members of a group through humiliating or dangerous initiation rituals. ---
examples: Some teams still haze their freshmen.
Two students said the fraternity hazed them for a week.
He was hazed so badly that he left the school.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with the noun haze (дымка); the -ing form hazing is the usual American word for the practice itself.

entries.meaning: To have or place a company's main offices in a particular location. ---
examples: Insurers often headquarter their operations in Delaware.
They headquartered the new division in Austin.
The airline is headquartered in Atlanta.
entries.contrast: Nearly always passive: the firm is headquartered in Dallas, not the firm headquarters in Dallas.

entries.meaning: To pile something up, or to give someone a great deal of praise or blame at once. ---
examples: Critics heap praise on every record she puts out.
He heaped his plate with fries.
Blame was heaped on the contractor.
entries.contrast: Often heap something on someone: heaped scorn on the plan.

entries.meaning: To protect yourself against a possible loss, or to avoid answering a question directly. ---
examples: Airlines hedge against sudden jumps in fuel prices.
He hedged when reporters asked about the deadline.
The fund has been hedging its currency exposure all year.
entries.русский: уклоняться от прямого ответа; страховаться, подстраховаться (от риска)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hedge their bets), intransitive (stop hedging and answer)

entries.meaning: To pay careful attention to advice or a warning and act on it. ---
examples: Few drivers heed the speed limit on that stretch.
The town heeded the evacuation order and got out early.
The engineers' warnings were never heeded.

entries.meaning: To bleed heavily, or, of an organization, to lose money or people at a damaging rate. ---
examples: Without a transfusion a patient can hemorrhage to death in minutes.
The airline hemorrhaged cash for three straight quarters.
She was hemorrhaging internally by the time they operated.
entries.русский: истекать кровью; терять в огромных количествах (деньги, сотрудников)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hemorrhaged cash), intransitive (the patient was hemorrhaging)
entries.contrast: American hemorrhage, British haemorrhage; note the double r, and the ending is just -ij: HEM-ur-ij.

entries.meaning: To make sudden sharp sounds in your throat that you cannot control. ---
examples: Babies hiccup constantly in the first few weeks.
He hiccuped all through the ceremony.
She has been hiccuping for nearly an hour.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one p — hiccuped, hiccuping; hiccupped and the old spelling hiccough are far less common.

entries.meaning: To travel by standing at the roadside and getting free rides from passing drivers. ---
examples: Students still hitchhike to the coast in the summer.
He hitchhiked from Denver to Seattle in four days.
She spent that whole year hitchhiking around Europe.

entries.meaning: To mix socially with important or wealthy people. ---
examples: Lobbyists hobnob with senators at these dinners.
He hobnobbed with the studio crowd all week.
She was hobnobbing with donors in the back room.
entries.русский: водить компанию (с влиятельными людьми), общаться запросто
entries.contrast: Doubles the b: hobnobbed, hobnobbing; always hobnob with someone.

entries.meaning: To take or use all of something, leaving none for anyone else. ---
examples: Don't hog the remote all night.
One speaker hogged the entire discussion.
He has been hogging the good chair since he got here.
entries.contrast: Doubles the g: hogged, hogging.

entries.meaning: To shout loudly, often to get someone's attention. ---
examples: Just holler if you need anything.
His father hollered at him from the driveway.
Somebody was hollering about a leak upstairs.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hollered a warning), intransitive (he hollered from the porch)

entries.meaning: To make all the parts of something the same, or to treat milk so that the cream does not separate. ---
examples: Chain stores homogenize every downtown they move into.
The dairy homogenized and pasteurized the milk the same morning.
Television has homogenized regional accents.
entries.contrast: American homogenize, British homogenise.

entries.meaning: To take the vacation a couple goes on right after their wedding. ---
examples: They plan to honeymoon in Iceland.
My parents honeymooned in a borrowed cabin.
The couple are honeymooning somewhere in Portugal.

entries.meaning: To trick someone by telling them something that is not true. ---
examples: These ads hoodwink people into signing long contracts.
The seller hoodwinked them about the condition of the roof.
Investors felt they had been hoodwinked.

entries.meaning: To chase or pester someone constantly and without mercy. ---
examples: Reporters hound anyone connected to the case.
Collection agencies hounded him for two years.
She was hounded out of her job.

entries.meaning: To make something feel more human, or to make people see someone as a real person. ---
