examples: Small details humanize a story like this.
The documentary humanized a man most people knew only from headlines.
Critics say the film is humanizing a dangerous figure.
entries.contrast: American humanize, British humanise.

entries.meaning: To make someone feel less important or less proud, often by defeating them. ---
examples: One bad season can humble even a great team.
The loss humbled a squad that had not lost all year.
I was humbled by how much help people offered.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: HUM-buhl.

entries.meaning: To bend your back and shoulders forward into a rounded shape. ---
examples: Don't hunch over your phone like that.
He hunched his shoulders against the wind.
Three of them were hunched around a laptop.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (hunch your shoulders), intransitive (he hunched over the desk)

entries.meaning: To move very fast, usually in a way that looks out of control. ---
examples: Rocks sometimes hurtle down onto the highway here.
The truck hurtled through the intersection.
The country is hurtling toward another shutdown.
entries.русский: нестись, мчаться; лететь на огромной скорости
entries.contrast: Not hurdle (барьер): a car hurtles down the road, a runner hurdles a barrier.

entries.meaning: Of a vehicle, to slide out of control on a film of water lying on the road. ---
examples: Worn tires hydroplane easily in heavy rain.
The van hydroplaned and spun into the median.
She lost control after hydroplaning on a flooded curve.
entries.русский: глиссировать, скользить по воде; терять сцепление с мокрой дорогой
entries.contrast: American drivers say hydroplane; British drivers say aquaplane.

entries.meaning: To promote something loudly and excessively in order to get attention for it. ---
examples: Studios hype every sequel as the biggest one yet.
The company hyped the launch for months.
The product was heavily hyped and then quietly canceled.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: hyping, not hypeing.

entries.meaning: To put someone into a sleeplike state in which they respond to suggestion, or to hold their attention completely. ---
examples: Stage acts hypnotize volunteers from the audience.
The therapist hypnotized him as part of the treatment.
The children sat hypnotized by the fish tank.
entries.contrast: American hypnotize, British hypnotise.

entries.meaning: To think of someone or something as better or more perfect than they really are. ---
examples: We all idealize the decade we grew up in.
The movie idealized small-town life.
Their marriage has been idealized by everyone who writes about it.
entries.contrast: American idealize, British idealise.

entries.meaning: To drink something, especially alcohol, or to take in ideas from the world around you. ---
examples: Guests who imbibe should hand over their car keys.
He imbibed his father's politics without ever questioning them.
They had clearly been imbibing before the meeting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (imbibe the local customs), intransitive (they had been imbibing all evening)

entries.meaning: To fill something or someone with a particular quality or feeling. ---
examples: A good teacher can imbue a class with real curiosity.
Her grandmother imbued her with a sense of duty.
The film is imbued with a quiet sadness.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: imbuing; usually imbue something with a quality.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something remembered forever, especially in art, writing, or film. ---
examples: Photographers immortalize moments that would otherwise be forgotten.
The song immortalized a small town in Kansas.
Her face has been immortalized on the ten-dollar bill.
entries.contrast: American spelling is immortalize; British writing uses immortalise.

entries.meaning: To have a strong effect on someone or something. ---
examples: Rising fuel prices impact every part of the economy.
The strike impacted deliveries for three weeks.
Sales have been badly impacted by the recall.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the cuts impacted every department), intransitive (the meteor impacted at enormous speed)
entries.contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, IM-pact; the verb on the second, im-PACT.

entries.meaning: To pierce something right through with a sharp, pointed object. ---
examples: Do not impale the steak with a fork, or the juices run out.
A branch impaled the tire and the car skidded off the road.
Receipts were impaled on a metal spike beside the register.

entries.meaning: To drive someone to act, usually because of a strong feeling or need. ---
examples: Curiosity impels scientists to ask uncomfortable questions.
Something impelled her to open the letter right away.
He felt impelled to speak up at the meeting.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the l doubles: impelled, impelling.

entries.meaning: To put someone or something in danger. ---
examples: New tariffs could imperil thousands of jobs.
The leak imperiled the whole investigation.
Several species are imperiled by the loss of wetlands.
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: imperiled, imperiling. British English doubles it: imperilled.

entries.meaning: To have an effect on something, especially by intruding on it or limiting it. ---
examples: The new rules impinge on the rights of tenants.
Work impinged on every weekend that spring.
She felt her privacy was being impinged upon.
entries.contrast: Always takes on or upon: impinge on your freedom, never impinge your freedom.

entries.meaning: To put something into a body or into someone's mind so that it stays there. ---
examples: Surgeons implant a small device just under the collarbone.
The ad campaign implanted the slogan in everyone's head.
A chip had been implanted under the dog's skin.
entries.contrast: The noun is IM-plant (the device); the verb is im-PLANT (the action).

entries.meaning: To collapse violently inward, or to fail suddenly and completely. ---
examples: Crews will implode the old hotel on Sunday morning.
The startup imploded after its funding fell through.
The tank had imploded under the pressure of the water.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (crews imploded the old stadium), intransitive (the company imploded)
entries.contrast: The opposite of explode: an implosion collapses inward rather than blowing outward.

entries.meaning: To beg someone earnestly to do something. ---
examples: I implore you to think it over before you sign anything.
She implored the judge for more time.
They had implored him not to drive in that weather.

entries.meaning: To force a rule, tax, or opinion on someone, or to take unfair advantage of someone's kindness. ---
examples: The state may impose a fine of up to a thousand dollars.
They imposed strict limits on water use.
Sanctions have been imposed on three more banks.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the city imposed a curfew), intransitive (I hope I am not imposing)
entries.contrast: Takes on: impose a tax on imports; I do not want to impose on you.

entries.meaning: To make a person, place, or thing poor or much weaker. ---
examples: A long war can impoverish a country for a generation.
The closing of the mine impoverished the entire valley.
Soil that has been impoverished by overfarming grows almost nothing.

entries.meaning: To soak something thoroughly with a substance, or to make a female pregnant. ---
examples: They impregnate the wood with a preservative before shipping it.
The rain impregnated the canvas with a musty smell.
The paper is impregnated with a chemical that turns blue in acid.

entries.meaning: To attack something as false, especially someone's honesty or motives. ---
examples: No one here is trying to impugn your integrity.
The defense impugned the witness's memory of that night.
His motives have been impugned in every editorial this week.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: im-PYOON, rhyming with soon.

entries.meaning: To say that someone or something is responsible for an action or quality, often unfairly. ---
examples: Do not impute motives to people you have never met.
The report imputed the delay to poor planning.
Income imputed from the rental has to be declared.
entries.contrast: Takes to: you impute something to someone.

entries.meaning: To make someone or something unable to work or function normally. ---
examples: A single blow to the knee can incapacitate a runner for months.
The flu incapacitated half the office in one week.
He was incapacitated by the injury and could not testify.

entries.meaning: To make someone extremely angry. ---
examples: Remarks like that incense the people who did the actual work.
The decision incensed fans across the country.
Parents were incensed by the sudden change to the schedule.
entries.contrast: The noun (the fragrant smoke) is IN-sens; the verb is in-SENS.

entries.meaning: To give someone a reward or advantage that encourages them to act in a particular way. ---
examples: Tax credits incentivize companies to hire locally.
The city incentivized builders with cheaper permits.
Recycling has been incentivized through a deposit on every bottle.
entries.contrast: American spelling is incentivize; British writing uses incentivise.

entries.meaning: To move very slowly, a little at a time. ---
examples: Just inch the couch to the left a few more feet.
The line inched forward for two hours.
Prices have been inching up since January.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he inched the car forward), intransitive (traffic inched along)

entries.meaning: To destroy something completely by burning it. ---
examples: The plant incinerates about two hundred tons of trash a day.
The fire incinerated everything in the storage unit.
Medical waste must be incinerated, not buried.

entries.meaning: To slope or lean, or to make someone tend toward a particular opinion or action. ---
examples: The ramp inclines gently toward the entrance.
Her calm tone inclined us to believe her.
I am inclined to wait another week before deciding.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the evidence inclines me to agree), intransitive (the roof inclines steeply)
entries.contrast: The noun is IN-cline (a slope); the verb is in-CLINE.

entries.meaning: To cause someone trouble or difficulty. ---
examples: I hope the change does not inconvenience you too much.
The detour inconvenienced thousands of commuters.
Passengers inconvenienced by the delay were offered vouchers.
entries.contrast: The silent e stays before -ing so the c keeps its soft sound: inconveniencing.

entries.meaning: To include something as part of a larger whole, or to form a legal corporation. ---
examples: Try to incorporate the reviewers' comments into the draft.
They incorporated the business in Nevada for tax reasons.
Several of her ideas were incorporated into the final design.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (incorporate the feedback), intransitive (the firm incorporated in Delaware)

entries.meaning: To increase a number or value by a fixed amount, usually by one. ---
examples: The loop increments the counter on every pass.
We incremented the version number before the release.
The build number is incremented automatically.

entries.meaning: To fix an idea or habit in someone's mind by repeating it often. ---
examples: Coaches try to inculcate discipline from the very first practice.
Her parents inculcated a love of reading early on.
Those values had been inculcated in him since childhood.

entries.meaning: To bring something unpleasant, especially a cost or a penalty, on yourself by your own actions. ---
examples: Late payments incur a fee of twenty dollars.
The team incurred heavy losses in the first quarter.
Any debt incurred before the marriage stays separate.
entries.contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles: incurred, incurring.

entries.meaning: To promise to pay someone back for any loss or damage they suffer. ---
examples: The contract requires the vendor to indemnify the city.
The insurer indemnified the family for the whole loss.
Volunteers are indemnified against claims arising from the event.
entries.contrast: The y becomes i before -es and -ed (indemnifies, indemnified) but stays before -ing (indemnifying).

entries.meaning: To formally charge someone with a serious crime. ---
examples: A grand jury can indict on far less evidence than a trial requires.
Prosecutors indicted four executives last spring.
He was indicted on charges of fraud.
entries.contrast: The c is silent: in-DYT, rhyming with night, not with strict.

entries.meaning: To adapt something so that it suits one particular person. ---
examples: Good teachers individualize the work for each student.
The clinic individualized her treatment after the second visit.
Every lesson plan here is individualized.
entries.contrast: American spelling is individualize; British writing uses individualise.

entries.meaning: To teach someone a set of beliefs so thoroughly that they accept them without question. ---
examples: Regimes indoctrinate children through the school system.
The group indoctrinated new members over several months.
He claimed he had been indoctrinated as a teenager.

entries.meaning: To persuade someone to act, or to cause a physical state to begin. ---
examples: Nothing could induce her to sell the house.
The drug induced a deep sleep within minutes.
Labor was induced two weeks early.
entries.contrast: Two quite different senses share one verb: persuasion (induce someone to do something, with a to-infinitive) and causation (induce sleep, induce vomiting), the second common in medicine. The noun is inducement for the first and induction for the second. Do not confuse it with deduce, which is to reason out.

entries.meaning: To develop factories and industry in a country or region on a large scale. ---
examples: Cheap energy helped the region industrialize.
Japan industrialized at remarkable speed.
Much of the coastline has been heavily industrialized.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the state industrialized the north), intransitive (the region industrialized quickly)
entries.contrast: American spelling is industrialize; British writing uses industrialise.

entries.meaning: To enter a place or organization secretly, usually to gather information or cause harm. ---
examples: It took two years to infiltrate the smuggling ring.
An undercover officer infiltrated the meeting.
The network had been infiltrated months earlier.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (agents infiltrated the group), intransitive (water infiltrates into the soil)

entries.meaning: To make a feeling, a conflict, or a part of the body worse and more painful or intense. ---
examples: Careless remarks can inflame an already tense situation.
The verdict inflamed protests across the city.
His knee was badly inflamed after the game.

entries.meaning: To change the form of a word to show tense, number, or case, or to change the pitch of your voice. ---
examples: Russian inflects nouns for six cases.
She inflected the last word so that it sounded like a question.
Most English adjectives are not inflected at all.
entries.русский: склонять, спрягать (изменять форму слова); менять интонацию
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (English inflects verbs for tense), intransitive (these nouns do not inflect)

entries.meaning: To cause someone to suffer something unpleasant, such as pain, damage, or a punishment. ---
examples: I would not inflict that movie on my worst enemy.
The storm inflicted millions of dollars in damage.
The wounds were inflicted with a blunt object.
entries.contrast: You inflict something on someone: inflict pain on a rival.

entries.meaning: To break a law or agreement, or to limit someone's rights unfairly. ---
examples: The design infringes two of our patents.
The company infringed on a trademark it had never heard of.
No right may be infringed without due process.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the design infringes two patents), intransitive (it infringes on his rights)
entries.contrast: Transitive with a patent or copyright, but on or upon with a right or freedom.

entries.meaning: To fill something with a quality or substance, or to soak something in liquid to draw out its flavor. ---
examples: A good director can infuse a tired script with real energy.
She infused the vinegar with chili peppers.
The cake was infused with lemon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (infuse the oil with garlic), intransitive (let the tea infuse)

entries.meaning: To take food, drink, or another substance into the body, usually by swallowing. ---
examples: Children can ingest lead from old paint chips.
The dog ingested something toxic in the yard.
The amount ingested was too small to cause harm.

entries.meaning: To fix a habit, belief, or attitude so firmly in someone that it becomes very hard to change. ---
examples: Years of drills ingrain the motion until you stop thinking about it.
The training ingrained a habit of checking everything twice.
Those attitudes are deeply ingrained in the culture.

entries.meaning: To try to make someone like you, usually by flattering them or doing them favors. ---
examples: He will do anything to ingratiate himself with the boss.
She ingratiated herself with the neighbors by shoveling their walk.
He spent the evening ingratiating himself with the investors.
entries.contrast: Always reflexive and followed by with: ingratiate yourself with someone.

entries.meaning: To live in a particular place. ---
examples: Only a few hundred people inhabit the island year-round.
Wolves once inhabited most of the state.
The cabin has not been inhabited since the fire.
entries.contrast: The last syllable is unstressed, so the t does not double: inhabited, not inhabitted (compare admit to admitted).

entries.meaning: To slow down or prevent a process, or to make someone feel unable to act freely. ---
examples: Cold weather inhibits the growth of the seedlings.
The camera inhibited everyone at the table.
Recovery was inhibited by a lack of sleep.
entries.contrast: The stress is on HIB, so the final t stays single: inhibited, inhibiting.

entries.meaning: To set something, especially a computer variable or a device, to its starting state. ---
examples: You have to initialize the array before you use it.
The script initialized the database with default settings.
The drive must be initialized before it will mount.
entries.contrast: American spelling is initialize; British writing uses initialise.

entries.meaning: To sign a contract or agreement, a use common in American sports and business reporting. ---
examples: The team hopes to ink a deal before the deadline.
She inked a two-year extension last month.
The agreement was inked in Geneva on Friday.

entries.meaning: To suggest something unpleasant indirectly rather than saying it openly. ---
examples: Are you trying to insinuate that I lied?
He insinuated that the results had been arranged in advance.
Nothing was said directly, but a great deal was insinuated.

entries.meaning: To create an actual instance of something general, especially an object from a class in programming. ---
examples: The factory method instantiates the right handler for each file type.
We instantiated the client once and reused it everywhere.
A new session is instantiated for every request.

entries.meaning: To bury a dead body, especially in a formal ceremony. ---
examples: The family chose to inter the ashes beside her parents.
They interred him with full military honors.
Hundreds of soldiers are interred in that cemetery.
entries.contrast: The r doubles: interred, interring. Do not confuse it with intern, which means to detain someone.

entries.meaning: To connect two or more things to each other so that they work together. ---
examples: Fiber lines interconnect all the campus buildings.
Engineers interconnected the two power grids last year.
Everything in the ecosystem is interconnected.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the cable interconnects the buildings), intransitive (the tunnels interconnect)

entries.meaning: To work together or communicate with another person, system, or device. ---
examples: The scanner interfaces with any standard laptop.
Our team interfaced directly with the client's engineers.
The two systems have never interfaced well.
entries.contrast: Takes with: interface with the payroll system.

entries.meaning: To fit two or more things together so that they hold each other in place. ---
examples: The bricks interlock without any mortar at all.
She interlocked her fingers and waited.
The panels are interlocked along every edge.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (interlock your fingers), intransitive (the pieces interlock)

entries.meaning: To marry someone from a different group, religion, or family. ---
examples: The two communities began to intermarry in the 1920s.
Settlers intermarried with the people already living there.
Their families had intermarried for generations.
entries.русский: заключать смешанные браки, вступать в брак между собой
entries.contrast: The y becomes i before -es and -ed (intermarries, intermarried) but stays before -ing (intermarrying).

entries.meaning: To mix together, or to mix things together, so that they are no longer separate. ---
examples: Guests from both parties began to intermingle around the bar.
Smoke intermingled with the fog over the river.
The two styles are thoroughly intermingled in her later work.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they intermingled the two flocks), intransitive (the crowds intermingled)

entries.meaning: To estimate a value that lies between two known values, or to insert something into a text. ---
examples: The software will interpolate the missing readings.
A later editor interpolated two lines into the poem.
Temperatures between stations are interpolated from the nearest sensors.

entries.meaning: To be connected to each other in a way that makes each one affect the other. ---
examples: The chapters interrelate more closely than they first appear to.
The study showed how sleep and mood interrelated.
Climate, soil, and crop yield are closely interrelated.

entries.meaning: To cross another line, road, or area, or to meet and cross each other. ---
examples: The two trails intersect just past the bridge.
A fire road intersected the path at the ridge.
Their careers have intersected several times.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the highway intersects the river), intransitive (the two lines intersect)

entries.meaning: To scatter things here and there among other things. ---
examples: Intersperse the photographs through the text instead of grouping them.
He interspersed the lecture with jokes.
The lawn is interspersed with wildflowers.
entries.contrast: Usually used with with: interspersed with quotations.

entries.meaning: To twist together, or to connect two things so closely that they cannot be separated. ---
examples: The vines intertwine along the whole length of the fence.
History intertwined the two families long before the wedding.
Their finances are hopelessly intertwined.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she intertwined the ribbons), intransitive (the vines intertwine)

entries.meaning: To suggest or hint at something rather than say it directly. ---
examples: He would not intimate how the vote might go.
She intimated that she might resign in the spring.
It had been intimated to us that the funding was at risk.
entries.contrast: The adjective (an intimate dinner) ends in -muht; the verb ends in -mayt: IN-tuh-mayt.

entries.meaning: To make someone drunk, or to excite someone so much that they cannot think clearly. ---
examples: Two drinks are enough to intoxicate someone that size.
Early success intoxicated the young band.
He was arrested for driving while intoxicated.

entries.meaning: To put a tube into a person's windpipe so that they can breathe. ---
examples: Paramedics may have to intubate at the scene.
Doctors intubated her within minutes of her arrival.
He spent nine days intubated in intensive care.

entries.meaning: To understand or know something by feeling rather than by reasoning or evidence. ---
examples: Good salespeople intuit what a customer actually wants.
She intuited right away that something was wrong.
The answer had been intuited long before anyone could prove it.

entries.meaning: To make someone so used to something unpleasant that it no longer bothers them. ---
examples: Years on the night shift inure you to the noise.
The work inured her to the sight of blood.
Residents have become inured to the sirens.
entries.contrast: Almost always passive and followed by to: be inured to hardship.

entries.meaning: To make a complete list of the goods or items in a place. ---
examples: Volunteers inventory the food pantry every Monday.
The staff inventoried everything in the warehouse.
All the equipment has been inventoried and tagged.
entries.contrast: The y becomes i before -es and -ed (inventories, inventoried) but stays before -ing (inventorying).

entries.meaning: To turn something upside down or reverse its order or position. ---
examples: Invert the pan over a plate and lift it straight off.
The question inverted the usual order of subject and verb.
The image is inverted by the lens.
entries.русский: переворачивать, перевернуть; менять порядок на обратный

entries.meaning: To put money, time, or effort into something in the hope of a return. ---
examples: They invest a fixed amount every month.
We invested four years in that project.
She has invested heavily in solar.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (invest the money), intransitive (invest in bonds)
entries.contrast: The preposition is in: invest in a company, never ✗ invest to a company. It works for time and effort as readily as for money, and the emotional sense is usually passive — I'm invested in how this turns out. Note the different noun forms: investment for the money, investor for the person.

entries.meaning: To give someone or something new energy and strength. ---
examples: A cold swim will invigorate you faster than coffee.
New leadership invigorated the whole department.
She came back from the trip looking invigorated.

entries.meaning: To call on a law, a right, or an authority as a reason or a source of support. ---
examples: Witnesses can invoke the Fifth Amendment and say nothing.
The governor invoked emergency powers the night of the flood.
The same clause has been invoked three times this year.
entries.contrast: You invoke a rule or a power, but you evoke a memory or a feeling.

entries.meaning: To have something as a necessary part or a necessary result. ---
examples: Does the job involve much travel?
The repair involved pulling out the whole engine.
It is a long process, involving three separate forms.

entries.meaning: To give atoms or molecules an electric charge by adding or removing electrons. ---
examples: Strong radiation can ionize the air inside the chamber.
The gas ionized the moment the voltage rose.
Hospitals limit how much ionizing radiation a patient receives.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (X-rays ionize the air), intransitive (the gas ionizes at high temperatures)
entries.contrast: American spelling is ionize; British writing uses ionise.

entries.meaning: To expose something to radiation, usually to kill germs or to treat a disease. ---
examples: Some countries irradiate imported fruit to kill insects.
The tumor was irradiated over six weeks.
The plant is irradiating spices around the clock.

entries.meaning: To list things one by one, especially the separate costs on a bill. ---
examples: Please itemize every expense on the form.
The mechanic itemized the parts and the labor.
We asked for an itemized receipt at checkout.
entries.contrast: American spelling is itemize; British writing uses itemise.

entries.meaning: To repeat a process, improving the result a little each time. ---
examples: Small studios iterate instead of waiting for a perfect plan.
We iterated on the layout until it finally felt right.
They have been iterating on the same screen all month.
entries.русский: дорабатывать версию за версией, повторять цикл
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they iterate the design weekly), intransitive (good teams iterate fast)
entries.contrast: Iterate means to repeat and improve; reiterate means to say something again.

entries.meaning: To talk fast and at length in a way that is hard to follow. ---
examples: The twins jabber at each other from morning to night.
He jabbered something about a missed connection and ran off.
She fell asleep with the radio jabbering in the corner.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he jabbered something about a delay), intransitive (they jabbered all the way home)

entries.meaning: For a truck and its trailer to fold sharply toward each other and go out of control. ---
examples: Empty trailers jackknife easily on black ice.
A semi jackknifed across two lanes of the interstate.
Traffic stopped behind a jackknifed tanker.
entries.русский: складываться пополам (о фуре с прицепом), сложиться
entries.contrast: The noun makes the plural jackknives, but the verb takes a plain -s: it jackknifes.

entries.meaning: To make a harsh ringing noise, the way loose metal does. ---
examples: Loose change jangles in his coat pocket.
The keys jangled as the guard walked past the cell.
Three cups of coffee left her nerves jangling.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he jangled his keys), intransitive (her bracelets jangled)

entries.meaning: To give something a sudden unpleasant shake or shock. ---
examples: Sirens jar him awake almost every night.
The hard landing jarred every passenger forward.
It was a jarring end to a very quiet evening.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the pothole jarred my back), intransitive (the color jars with the rest of the room)
entries.contrast: The consonant doubles: jar → jarred, jarring.

entries.meaning: To cross a street illegally, away from a crosswalk or against the light. ---
examples: People jaywalk all over midtown at lunchtime.
She jaywalked to catch the bus before it pulled away.
He got a forty-dollar ticket for jaywalking.

entries.meaning: To come together into something that finally works, such as a team, a plan, or an idea. ---
examples: Give the group a month and they will jell.
The offense finally jelled in the second half.
Her argument was still jelling when the deadline hit.
entries.contrast: Also written gel in American English; both spellings sound the same.

entries.meaning: To put something valuable at risk of being lost or damaged. ---
examples: One careless email could jeopardize the whole deal.
The delay jeopardized their visa applications.
Funding has been jeopardized by the audit.
entries.русский: ставить под угрозу, подвергать опасности; поставить под угрозу
entries.contrast: American spelling is jeopardize; British writing uses jeopardise.

entries.meaning: To move, or to move something, with one short sudden pull. ---
examples: Never jerk the wheel on an icy road.
He jerked his hand back from the hot pan.
The elevator started jerking between floors.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she jerked the rope), intransitive (the train jerked forward)

entries.meaning: To throw away or abandon something you no longer want or can no longer carry. ---
examples: Pilots jettison fuel before an emergency landing.
The party jettisoned the proposal as soon as the polls came out.
Half the schedule was jettisoned to save money.

entries.meaning: To agree with something else or fit together with it. ---
examples: These numbers do not jibe with last quarter's report.
His account jibed with what the neighbors told police.
The two timelines were not jibing, so we checked again.
entries.contrast: Jibe takes with, and it is a different word from gibe (to mock) and jive (music, or nonsense talk).

entries.meaning: To move, or make something move, with quick short shakes. ---
examples: Jiggle the key a little and the lock opens.
He jiggled the handle until the toilet stopped running.
The dashboard was jiggling the whole way down the gravel road.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (jiggle the key), intransitive (the mirror jiggles)

entries.meaning: To suddenly end a romance with someone you were expected to marry. ---
examples: Nobody expects a groom to jilt the bride an hour before the ceremony.
She jilted him by text message.
The jilted fiancé kept the ring and the deposit.

entries.meaning: To force a lock, door, or window open with a bar or a tool. ---
examples: A thief can jimmy that window in about ten seconds.
Someone jimmied the back door and took two laptops.
He was caught jimmying the latch with a screwdriver.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie before -s and -d (jimmies, jimmied) but stays in jimmying.

entries.meaning: To make a light ringing sound, like small bells or loose coins. ---
examples: Coins jingle in the donation box by the door.
The dog's tags jingled all the way down the hallway.
He walked in jingling a set of car keys.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he jingled the coins), intransitive (the bells jingle)

entries.meaning: To bring bad luck to someone or something, often by mentioning it too soon. ---
examples: Do not jinx it — there are still two innings left.
I said the word shutout and jinxed the whole game.
This car feels jinxed.
entries.contrast: The third person adds -es: he jinxes it every time.

entries.meaning: To maneuver for advantage, especially by pushing past rivals. ---
examples: Six candidates jockey for the same endorsement every spring.
The two firms jockeyed for the contract all year.
Reporters were jockeying for a spot near the podium.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he jockeyed the truck into the loading bay), intransitive (six candidates jockey for the same seat)
entries.contrast: A vowel comes before the -y, so it stays: jockeyed, not jockied.

entries.meaning: To write regularly in a personal diary about your thoughts and your days. ---
examples: She journals for ten minutes before work.
I journaled through the whole move.
Journaling helped him think the decision through.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she journals her dreams), intransitive (he journals every morning)
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: journaled, journaling; British writing doubles it.

entries.meaning: To travel, especially over a long distance. ---
examples: Thousands journey to the coast every summer.
The family journeyed west by wagon in 1847.
He spent two years journeying through South America.
entries.contrast: The -ey stays: journeyed, never journied.

entries.meaning: To fight on horseback with lances, or, in a figurative sense, to spar with someone in argument. ---
examples: Knights joust at the fair every July.
The two senators jousted for an hour on live television.
He enjoys jousting with reporters after a game.

entries.meaning: To squeeze the liquid out of fruit or vegetables, or informally to boost something. ---
examples: Juice two lemons for the dressing.
The rebate was meant to juice holiday spending.
She has been juicing carrots and beets every morning.

entries.meaning: To mix things together so that they end up in no order at all. ---
examples: Do not jumble the receipts — I sorted them by month.
The move jumbled everything in the garage.
Her notes were jumbled together in one folder.

entries.meaning: To get something moving quickly, or to start a car using cables from another battery. ---
examples: A tax rebate could jumpstart consumer spending.
A neighbor jumpstarted my car in the parking lot.
They are jumpstarting the project with outside money.
entries.русский: дать толчок, запустить; завести от другого аккумулятора
entries.contrast: Often written with a hyphen: jump-start.

entries.meaning: To throw something away as worthless, or to drop a plan entirely. ---
examples: We should junk the old printer and buy a new one.
The city junked the plan after the hearing.
Two hundred buses were junked last year.

entries.meaning: To stick out past a surface or an edge. ---
examples: Sharp rocks jut from the water at low tide.
A nail jutted up through the board.
The balcony, jutting out over the street, blocked all the light.
entries.contrast: The consonant doubles: jut → jutted, jutting.

entries.meaning: To put two things side by side so that the difference between them shows.
examples: Good editors juxtapose the two photographs on purpose.
The film juxtaposed wealth and poverty on the same block.
Juxtaposing the drafts shows how much he cut.
